nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; short-story writer, novelist and editor writing in English
literary_identity: American short-story writer and collagist, the most inventive practitioner of American postmodern fiction, whose hundred-odd stories in The New Yorker remade the short story as a structure of jokes, quotations and interruptions
biography: Donald Barthelme Jr. was born in Philadelphia on 7 April 1931, the son of an architect, and grew up in Houston, Texas, where his father taught at the University of Houston. He studied journalism there, wrote for the Houston Post, founded and edited the literary magazine Forum, was drafted into the army in 1953 and served in Korea as editor of an army newspaper, and in 1961 became director of the Contemporary Arts Museum in Houston, the year he published his first story. He was managing editor of Location and a co-founder of Fiction, and from 1963 The New Yorker published more than a hundred of his stories. Come Back, Dr. Caligari (1964) collected the first of them; Snow White (1967), first serialised in The New Yorker, was his first novel, followed by Unspeakable Practices, Unnatural Acts (1968), City Life (1970), the children's book The Slightly Irregular Fire Engine (1971, National Book Award 1972), Sadness (1972), Guilty Pleasures (1974), The Dead Father (1975), Amateurs (1976), Great Days (1979), Sixty Stories (1981), Overnight to Many Distant Cities (1983), Paradise (1986), Forty Stories (1987) and The King (1990, posthumous). He taught at Boston University, the University at Buffalo and the City College of New York, where he was distinguished visiting professor in 1974-75, and died of throat cancer in Houston on 23 July 1989.
literary_profile: Stories: Come Back, Dr. Caligari (1964), Unspeakable Practices, Unnatural Acts (1968), City Life (1970), Sadness (1972), Amateurs (1976), Great Days (1979), Sixty Stories (1981), Overnight to Many Distant Cities (1983), Forty Stories (1987), Flying to America (2008) and Collected Stories (2021). Novels: Snow White (1967), The Dead Father (1975), Paradise (1986) and The King (1990). Non-fiction and satire: Guilty Pleasures (1974), The Teachings of Don B. (1992) and Not-Knowing (1997). Children's book: The Slightly Irregular Fire Engine (1971).
stylistic_characteristics: Stories without plot in the traditional sense, built by accumulation and juxtaposition; the non-sequitur as a structural device; parody of found forms - the questionnaire, the catalogue, the academic essay, the newspaper column, the interview; dialogue of great flatness and precision; typographic and visual play; a deadpan narrator who reports the absurd as though it were ordinary.
intellectual_concerns: The making of art and the reception of the artwork by a public that wants it explained; the arbitrariness of the signs and objects among which Americans live; marriage, divorce and desire conducted in a language of cliché; the city as a grid and as a joke; death, and the difficulty of saying anything true about it; the exhaustion of inherited literary forms and the freedom that exhaustion offers.
historical_significance: Barthelme is the representative American postmodernist and the writer through whom the American short story after 1965 is usually periodised; his stories are standard anthology and workshop texts, 'The Balloon' and 'The School' are among the most widely reprinted American short stories of the postwar decades, and his influence is acknowledged by writers as different as George Saunders, David Foster Wallace and Lydia Davis. The Library of America collected his stories in 2021, the first such volume for a postwar American experimental short-story writer.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Barthelme and on his bibliography, read directly, with the first periodical printings of the two Norton selections taken from The New Yorker's own archive and from the bibliography's tables; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records the two Norton selections - 'The Balloon' (The New Yorker, 16 April 1966; collected 1968) and 'The School' (The New Yorker, 17 June 1974; collected 1976) - so the novels, the other hundred stories and the non-fiction have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.
